$comment: S-183 DRAFT — the walk table's DECLARED columns, scored on both halves.
🔴 WHAT THIS PINS, AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT.
The two halves render different SHAPES: `client2/src/walk/derive.js tableColumns`
returns one section PER TYPE and decorates it with fixed columns whose names are
Korean display text (깊이 · 라벨 · id · 충돌); the server's `format=rows` is ONE TSV
table whose fixed columns are machine names (type · depth · id · parent_id · via ·
seed · path · path_ids). Those two lists can never be equal, and a vector asserting
they are would be a vector nobody can satisfy.
What IS one rule, and is what these cases score: for a single type, which DECLARED
names become columns and IN WHAT ORDER —
the declaration's `keys`, then the QUALIFIER names the response actually carried,
then the declaration's `attributes`.
🔴 NO NAME IS WRITTEN ON EITHER SIDE. A key added to a declaration must add a column
to both the screen and the TSV with no edit in either — that is the property these
vectors exist to keep, and `unknown_type` is the case that proves the rule reads the
declaration rather than the response.
⚠️ THE UNION IS THE SERVER'S OWN. A TSV has one header, so the server merges the
per-type lists in the order the types were reached and leaves a cell blank where a
type never declared that column. The client has sections and needs no union. That
merge is therefore NOT scored here — only the per-type rule above, which the merge is
built out of.
⚠️ DRAFT: the server half reads these today (`_declared_columns`). The client half and
the harness that scores it are the lead's to place (S-183 order).

🔴 THE NODE TYPE IS BARE AND THE DECLARATION KEY IS VERSIONED — `declaration_key` carries that asymmetry, because it is the product's and scoring against a symmetric fixture is how a lookup that matched NOTHING passed every case here.

per_type_declared_columns.name: keys_only
per_type_declared_columns.$why: The commonest shape: a type whose identity is its only declared column.

per_type_declared_columns.name: keys_in_declared_order
per_type_declared_columns.$why: Declaration order, never sorted — the order is part of the answer, and a table that alphabetised it would separate x from y.

per_type_declared_columns.name: qualifiers_follow_keys
per_type_declared_columns.$why: A qualifier is what the ANSWER carried, not what the declaration promised, so it cannot come from the same list — but it still sits after identity.

per_type_declared_columns.name: attributes_come_last
per_type_declared_columns.$why: 🔴 Attributes are declared values that are NOT identity (setup_bundle says so where the grammar is defined), so they read after both.

per_type_declared_columns.name: all_three_groups
per_type_declared_columns.$why: The load-bearing case: keys → qualifiers → attributes, each group internally in its own declared order.

per_type_declared_columns.name: no_attributes_declared_adds_nothing
per_type_declared_columns.$why: ⚠️ An empty `attributes` must render byte-identically to a type that declares none — the client's conflicts column keys off `attributes.length` for the same reason.

per_type_declared_columns.name: unknown_type_declares_nothing
per_type_declared_columns.$why: 🔴 THE SENSITIVITY CONTROL. A type with no declaration contributes only what the response actually carried. An implementation that invented columns from the response's `keys` would pass every case above and fail this one.
